I think that default communities should be as free as other communities to implement community rules. Subverse rules needn't be arbitrary (and in fact shouldn't be). Moderators aren't policemen, but they aren't just janitors that clean up spam either. If a default community decides that it needs a rule to address a specific problem, the community is free to discuss that need and voice their desire for a specific and well-defined rule.

Moderating for a community isn't about being a policeman, but it's not about being a janitor either. Moderating for a community (even a default community) is an equal partnership between mods and community. Mods are tasked with facilitating the community's will and helping the subverse be whatever the community wants it to be.

/v/gaming is an excellent example. I moderate over there, but before I joined the modteam (and before the first Reddit exodus) the community at /v/gaming decided that they didn't want to be a clone of Reddit's /r/gaming, so they implemented a few community rules. One of those rules is no memes, so /v/gamingpics was created to facilitate that content. Another problem with Reddit's /r/gaming is that people would post content without specifying the game the content is from, prompting questions of "what game is this" in every thread and making it harder to find game-related content in search. For that reason, the community created rule 2, which asks that all posts include a game name in the title when necessary.

My job as a /v/gaming moderator is to respect the community's wishes and help to enforce their rules. Since all of my actions depend on the rules and their definitions, it's in my best interest to make sure those rules are as neatly defined and specific as possible so that I'm not making a judgement call every time I enforce them. For that reason, /v/gaming's rules were created with much feedback from the community and are very tightly defined. Terms like "clickbait" and "sustained harassment" are defined and stated, so that the rules are as impartial as possible, as clear as possible, and most importantly, as predictable as possible.

Part of my job means removing posts that break those community rules. When I have to remove a rule-breaking post (the title rule, for example) I'll try to get to it within a few minutes of it being posted, and work with the OP to get it redone with the community's rules in mind. If I can't get to a post in time and it receives upvoats or comments, I'll make due with a friendly rule reminder for next time; I consider it my fault for not catching the post quick enough, and no reason to remove someone's ongoing discussion when a reminder will be seen by more people due to the post's popularity.

If I had to pin down a closer approximation to a mod's role other than policeman or janitor, I'd say it's a lot like tech support or a help desk. It's equal parts enforcement and assistance, and it's always ultimately up to the community's wishes what rules should exist and how they should be enforced. Good moderating should reflect the community's wishes for itself, and that can be a greatly positive thing.

For example, posts without game names tend to be downvoated. There's no problem with that, but OP of a post might not realize why their post is being downvoated. Instead of just being downvoated, a post will attract the attention of one of /v/gaming's mods who can work with the user, explain the community's rules, and help to get that post redone in a way that will attract positive attention as long as the content is good.

Edit: I'd like to include a section from one of my posts when this subject came up about a year ago and I was new to the mod team:

That's not our only job, of course. Mods work as support to assist users wherever possible. About a month ago we had a user post some very nice fan art that unfortunately didn't include the game title in the post. One of our mods got to it early, worked with the user to understand the community's rules and helped them get the fanart repostsed with the game name in the title. Sure, we could just rely on downvotes to enforce the community's wishes, but having a dedicated support role meant the user was assisted directly instead of frustrated, and continues to post great fan art since. On another occasion a user made a post about a game that they enjoy but didn't indicate the game in the title either. These posts are usually ignored at best and downvoated at worst, and the poster might not understand why. One of the mods worked with them to repost their submission and it ended up being so popular that the developers of the game made an account in order to drop in and say hi.

So while not every community agrees that it even needs mods, the community of /v/gaming has given us a clear role and we work hard to support and respect the wishes of the community, and we've had relatively little drama for such a large sub. Our modlog showcases a history of respectful interactions and action backed up by clearly defined rules, which appears to be what was applied in this case as well.
